newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Pat Boone - crooner in a heavy metal mood.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pat Boone - crooner in a heavy metal mood.

text.p: Deep Purple, AC/DC, Led Zeppelin, Van Halen -- and now please add to the pantheon of HEAVY METAL ROCKERS the name of ... Pat Boone.

The 62-year-old pop crooner with the squeaky-clean image has just released what must be one of the weirdest albums in an already bizarre world of rock music. "Pat Boone In a Metal Mood: No More Mr Nice Guy" features the finger-snapping singer tackling some of the classics of heavy metal, from Zeppelin's "Stairway to Heaven" to Purple's "Smoke on the Water," but with a difference: A swinging big-band sound.

"These songs are well-constructed, melodic, harmonic gems," Boone told Reuters at his Sunset Boulevard office. "I'm totally ignorant of metal because, up till ... four years ago, any time I'm tuning across the (radio) dial and I hear what I assume is heavy metal or hard rock it's so jangly, distorted, raucous, angry, that it set my teeth on edge and I immediately went to something else."

Boone, who rocketed to fame in the pre-Beatles, Elvis era of the late 1950's and early 1960's, has had 18 Top Ten pop hits including "Love Letters in the Sand," "Ain't That a Shame," "I Almost Lost My Mind" and "April Love."
DID GREAT "TUTTI-FRUTTI"

But it was his sanitized version of Little Richard's "Tutti-Frutti" and Fats Domino tunes that helped so-called "race music" cross over to be accepted by white audiences. For that reason alone, he describes himself as "the midwife at the birth of rock 'n roll."
Nevertheless, rock is essentially a young people's music, so how did a grandfather with a successful career on the cabaret circuit and a clean-cut image get into heavy metal?

"It started as a joke in England ... my musicians, younger guys, were sitting around between planes on a tour. And the guys said 'Let's go in the studio, make a record, do something together.' They'd been playing my golden oldies for years.

"And I said 'Fellas, what do you think I could do that I haven't already done ten times over? I've done country, gospel, folk, pop, rock, movie themes, I mean what else can I do?' And one of them jokingly said 'Well, you never did any heavy metal.'"

"So we laughed because the idea was absurd." But Dave Siebels, Boone's conductor and arranger, told him about terrific songs that only metal-heads know and said, "If we were to do them a different way we might have something."
Boone had never heard the songs and asked Siebels to make a tape. That's when Boone got hooked.

"I started to get into it. Over the last two years I've bought a couple of hundred CD's and listened to them diligently. Groups like Motorhead, Megadeth, Scorpions and Vipers and KISS," he said. "I never dreamed I would go into a record store and buy all these things and of course I take 'em home and hide them."
A CONVERT TO "DEVIL'S MUSIC"
Now Boone, who has a strong sense of faith and has been associated with Christian music, is a convert to what was once called "the devil's music" and he wants to spread the word.

"If I'm in the music business and I had a real block about metal there must be millions and millions of people like me who have been turned off by the images of the lifestyle and the way these guys comport themselves and just the sheer decibel level," he said.

As a result of this project, he has come to know many of those metal-head musicians. "Smoke on the Water" even features Deep Purple's Ritchie Blackmore on solo guitar along with Dweezil Zappa, and Ronnie James Dio sings with Boone on "Holy Diver."

The album also features a version of Jimi Hendrix's "And the Wind Cries Mary," Judas Priest's "You've Got Another Thing Comin'," Alice Cooper's "No More Mr Nice Guy" and AC/DC's "It's a Long Way to the Top (If You Wanna Rock 'n Roll)."

Boone's only real concern is the reaction of his fans. "I may have been kidding in the idea but I'm dead serious about the music," he said. He said his grandchildren were thrilled about the album but one of his four daughters, singer Debbie, who had the hit "You Light Up My Life," had mixed feelings.
"She was guarded, thinking I might be devastated (by the reaction). But that's before she heard it. When she heard it she was very impressed by the music."
Boone himself has no doubts his "metal mood" will be a hit -- he has already recorded Volume 2.
